subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student finishes all class assignments well ahead of peers, asks unusually probing questions, and shows an intense curiosity across multiple subjects, often getting bored with routine drill work. Such a child is best described as:
explanation: Gifted children show significantly above-average intellectual ability, creativity, and task commitment; the appropriate response is enrichment or acceleration, not remedial teaching.

subject: Educational Psychology
stem: For a gifted child who has already mastered the current syllabus, the most appropriate teaching strategy is:

options.option_text: Enrichment activities and acceleration — offering deeper, more challenging or advanced material
Repeating the same grade-level content until the whole class catches up
Reducing the syllabus to only the bare minimum expected of average students
Ignoring the child's needs since they will manage on their own

explanation: Gifted education relies on enrichment (going deeper/broader) and acceleration (moving faster/ahead) so gifted learners remain challenged and engaged, rather than left idle with already-mastered content.

subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A child has below-average but not intellectually disabled ability (IQ roughly 70-90), takes longer than peers to grasp new concepts, but can eventually learn the same content with extra time, repetition, and simpler steps. This child is best classified as a:

options.option_text: Child with a specific learning disability

explanation: Slow learners have generally below-average ability across the board (unlike specific learning disabilities, which affect only certain skills despite normal intelligence) but are distinct from intellectual disability, which involves much greater deficits in adaptive functioning.

subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A written document prepared for a child with a disability, specifying the child's present level of performance, specific learning goals, required accommodations, and the special services to be provided, is known as a/an:
explanation: An IEP is a legally-grounded, individualised plan (mandated under the RPWD Act 2016 for children with disabilities) tailoring goals, accommodations, and support to a specific child's needs — distinct from generic assessment tools like CCE.
